teaser_en: The 2025 offense in advanced stats: an exceptionally efficient passing game under Brock Purdy and a run game that was only average.
body_en:
*Season Stats 2025, part 2 of 4. The series by Chris Pracher: Part 1: Understanding advanced stats · **Part 2: Season Stats 2025, offense deep dive** · Part 3: Defense deep dive · Part 4: All advanced stats at a glance.*

## Purdy carries, the run game wobbles: the 49ers' 2025 offense in an advanced stats check

Anyone who measures the San Francisco 49ers' 2025 offense only by yards and points misses the real story, because the advanced stats paint a much more honest picture, and it is one with two faces. On one side is a passing game that ranked among the very most efficient in the entire league, led by a quarterback who was simply No. 1 in the decisive metrics. On the other side is a run game that produced only mediocrity despite big names in the backfield. How does that fit together?

Key finding: Brock Purdy led the league in EPA/play and success rate in 2025, and the offense ranked second in the NFL in DVOA. The only real construction site was the run game.

## The big picture: elite through the air

Let's start with the bird's-eye view, because it frames everything else. Offensive EPA was +0.108 per play (rank 6), which is already a very good value, but the devil is in the breakdown. In the passing game, San Francisco produced +0.200 EPA/play (rank 5) with a success rate of 53.7 percent (rank 3), so it was not only explosive but above all reliably consistent, staying "on schedule." The most meaningful team number, however, comes from FTN's DVOA, which fully adjusts for opponent strength: at +17.6 percent, the offense ranked second in the entire NFL. Only a single team was more efficient. Considering that Brock Purdy missed eight games and the receiver room lost player after player, this ranking is almost uncanny; behind it shines the class of Kyle Shanahan's play-calling.

The break comes in the run game: there, EPA/play drops to -0.028 (rank 12), and the rushing success rate is only 42.8 percent (rank 11). For a team that has been celebrated for years for its zone scheme and run game, that is a sobering snapshot. In short: in 2025, this offense rode on the arm of its passing game. So let's talk about the man who conducted it.

## Brock Purdy: No. 1 in the most important numbers

There is an ongoing debate about whether Brock Purdy is a true franchise quarterback or just a game manager, and the advanced stats of the 2025 season give a remarkably clear answer. In the gold standard EPA/play (adjusted for garbage time), Purdy led the entire league at +0.328, first place overall. The success rate confirms it at 56.7 percent, also rank 1: in 2025 he was not only the most efficient but also the most consistent quarterback in the NFL. Anyone who leads both at the same time hasn't been lucky but has played at an MVP level.

The evidence keeps piling up. A CPOE of +7.2 (rank 2) shows that Purdy squeezed balls into windows that were too tight for the average quarterback; an ESPN QBR of 72.8 (rank 2) and a DVOA of +29.5 percent (rank 2) reinforce the picture from every direction. Probably most telling, though, is his pressure-to-sack rate of 9.0 percent, the best in the league: when Purdy came under pressure, he rarely turned it into a sack, a factor that was worth its weight in gold in a season in which the interior offensive line wobbled in pass blocking.

Where does Purdy have room to improve? Two numbers stand out. His big-time throw rate of 4.2 percent (rank 22) shows that he is not a quarterback who decides a game single-handedly with spectacular hero balls, and his turnover-worthy play rate of 3.7 percent (rank 15) is solid but not flawless. The overall picture, however, is crystal clear: in 2025, Purdy was one of the three or four best quarterbacks in the NFL. And his backup convinced as well: over the eight games without Purdy, Mac Jones posted +0.184 EPA/play (rank 9) and a DVOA of +19.0 percent (rank 8), a main reason why the offense never collapsed despite the absences.

|---|---|---|

| Success rate | 56.7% | 1 |
| Pressure-to-sack rate | 9.0% | 1 |
| DVOA | +29.5% | 2 |
| ESPN QBR | 72.8 | 2 |
| CPOE | +7.2 | 2 |

## Money downs: Purdy makes league history on 3rd and 4th down

How solid Purdy's season really was only becomes clear where it hurts the most, namely on 3rd and 4th down, when an offense has no second chance and every miss ends the drive. And precisely in this situation, in which many otherwise strong quarterbacks crack under the increased pressure, Purdy produced in 2025 perhaps the best money-down season the league has seen since the start of the modern play-by-play era.

Among all quarterbacks with at least 70 plays on 3rd/4th down, Purdy led the entire league with +0.611 adjusted EPA/play, clearly ahead of Joe Burrow (+0.577) and Jordan Love (+0.482), but the real outlier is the success rate: 62.1 percent. No other quarterback in the field came anywhere near that mark, and it fits with a CPOE of 14.3, which shows that in exactly these do-or-die moments, Purdy hit throws that statistically should have failed much more often than they did.

Historical context: a look at the RBSDM database going back to 2002 shows that before Purdy, no quarterback had ever cracked a 60 percent success rate on 3rd/4th down; the leader so far was Drew Brees in 2011 at 58.9 percent. Purdy's 62.1 percent is more than three percentage points higher and marks the first value above the 60 percent threshold in at least 24 years. In adjusted EPA/play, too, Purdy joins the most exclusive company: only Brees, Carson Wentz (2017) and Patrick Mahomes (2018) had previously exceeded +0.6 EPA/play in this situation.

What frames this value further is the context in which it was achieved. An average of 9.4 air yards on 3rd/4th down is not a value you reach with short screen designs or simple YAC concepts in short-yardage situations, but rather an indication that Purdy played a large share of these snaps in genuine 3rd-and-long scenarios, where deeper routes are needed to cover the full distance at all. Anyone who still reaches a 62.1 percent success rate under these conditions is clearly not relying on simple, easy-to-execute play designs but is repeatedly making the harder decision into the window.

How much this depends on the quarterback's individual class rather than the system is shown by a direct look at Mac Jones, who in 2025 went through exactly the same situation in exactly the same offense, under the same play-caller and with the same concepts. And there the difference is even clearer than in the overall season picture: on 3rd/4th down, Jones posted adjusted EPA/play of only +0.131 (rank 15) with a success rate of just 45.9 percent, more than 16 percentage points behind Purdy's 62.1 percent. Same scheme architecture, same play designs, yet on exactly the downs that keep a drive alive or end it, there is a gap of almost half a point between the two quarterbacks. That is probably one of the clearer indications that Purdy's money-down dominance is not purely a function of Shanahan's play-calling but rests largely on his own decision-making under pressure.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | B. Purdy | SFO | 103 | +0.611 | 62.1% | 14.3 | 56.4% | 9.4 |
| 2 | J. Burrow | CIN | 86 | +0.577 | 54.7% | 16.4 | 57.2% | 9.6 |
| 3 | J. Love | GB | 166 | +0.482 | 54.8% | 4.6 | 57.1% | 11.7 |

## Kittle, McCaffrey and the big receiver puzzle

Purdy had good targets, but not across the board, and of all things the two best were not classic wide receivers. At the top, as usual, was tight end George Kittle, whose 2.11 yards per route run (rank 3) exceeded the elite mark of 2.0 and whose ESPN tracking score of 76 was the best of all tight ends in the league. Kittle is and remains one of the best receiving tight ends in the NFL, and the numbers leave no doubt about it.

The most fascinating finding of the entire offensive analysis, however, concerns Christian McCaffrey, and it comes in two parts. As a pass catcher, CMC was phenomenal in 2025: EPA/target of +0.25 (rank 3), 1.81 yards per route run (rank 3), a target share of 23.45 percent (the highest on the team and first in the league) and a flat-out ESPN tracking score of 99 (rank 1). Out of the backfield, he was effectively this offense's No. 1 receiver, and fittingly, no NFL team threw to its running backs as often as San Francisco, where 31 percent of all passes went to the backs.

On the ground, however, the same player tells a completely different story. EPA per rushing attempt was -0.09 (rank 29), the rushing success rate 40.2 percent (rank 29), and perhaps the harshest number is an RYOE of -0.5 (rank 45): in 2025, McCaffrey got less out of the situations his line created for him than an average back would have. Before jumping to conclusions: his 50 forced missed tackles (rank 11) show that the pure elusiveness was still there. But the big chunk runs, once his trademark, came less often. The honest reading is: in 2025, McCaffrey was an elite receiving back and only an average runner; his value came through the air, not on the ground.

Among the actual wide receivers, the picture is mixed. Ricky Pearsall took steps forward with an EPA/target of +0.44 (rank 13), even if his separation of 2.6 yards (rank 66) shows that he didn't always get open easily. The case of Jauan Jennings is more critical: despite a target share of 19.4 percent, his efficiency numbers dropped significantly (EPA/target of -0.08, rank 65; 1.35 yards per route run, rank 62). A negative EPA/target at that volume is a warning sign; in 2025, San Francisco lacked a true second separator alongside Kittle and the receiving McCaffrey.

## The offensive line: elite in the run game, shaky in interior pass protection

If the run game only reached ranks 11 to 12 even though the line shone in run blocking, that raises questions, and part of the answer lies with the running backs, not up front. Because the run block grades were outstanding: left tackle Trent Williams reached 92.0 (rank 2) and right tackle Colton McKivitz 90.4 (rank 4), almost identical elite values, and the unit as a whole posted a run block win rate of 72 percent (rank 12). The line created holes; they just weren't always used optimally.

In pass protection, the picture is more nuanced. The collective pass blocking efficiency of 85.2 (rank 18) was exactly league average, and while Williams remained elite with a pass block grade of 80.3 (rank 7), center Jake Brendel (62.5) and guard Dominick Puni (63.3) struggled in the interior with below-average grades. That explains exactly why Purdy came under pressure so often, and why his league-best pressure-to-sack rate was so decisive in the end. Purdy bailed out an interior line that didn't always keep him clean in pass protection.

## Conclusion: a clear blueprint for 2026

Putting the pieces together, the 2025 offense forms a remarkably coherent picture: a top-5 passing offense, led by a quarterback who led the entire league in EPA/play and success rate, with the best tight end at his position and a league-wide elite receiving back whose ground game, however, was only average anymore. For 2026 roster planning, the blueprint almost writes itself: a second reliable separator in the passing game, fresh legs in the backfield for explosiveness on the ground, and reinforcements in the interior of the offensive line. But the foundation, the quarterback, is in place. And it holds.

Go Niners!

### Methodology glossary: what the metrics mean

**EPA/play:** Source: RBSDM / Sumersports. Sum of all EPA on dropbacks or plays, divided by their number: the gold standard of efficiency per play, cleaned of the noise of pure volume stats. The league average is around 0.0.

**Success rate:** Source: RBSDM / Sumersports. Share of plays with positive EPA (or ≥40% of the needed yards on 1st down, 60% on 2nd, 100% on 3rd/4th): measures consistency rather than magnitude.

**Pressure-to-sack rate:** Source: PFF / SIS. Share of plays under pressure that turn into a sack; low means good pocket presence.

**DVOA:** Source: FTN Football Almanac (originally Aaron Schatz, Football Outsiders). Compares every play with the league average in the same situation and adjusts for opponent strength.

**ESPN QBR:** Source: ESPN Analytics. EPA-based across all QB actions, opponent-adjusted, without garbage time; scale 0–100, 70+ is considered elite.

**CPOE:** Source: RBSDM. Actual completion rate minus expected rate (from pass distance, separation, pressure, defender proximity): pure accuracy.

**Adj. EPA/play (money down):** Source: RBSDM. EPA/play on 3rd/4th down, weighted by win probability to reduce garbage-time distortions.

**YPRR:** Source: PFF. Receiving yards divided by routes run; above 2.0 very good, above 2.5 elite.

**Target share:** Source: Sumersports. Targets divided by all team targets in the games in which the player was active.

**ESPN tracking:** Source: ESPN Advanced Stats. Composite 0–99 of open score, catch score and YAC score; 99 is absolute elite.
